736.title: Bilal, "One, One"
736.hook: Umayyah lays a rock on Bilal in the sun, and he says only ahad
736.howItsDone: Muslims honor Bilal as an early companion and remember his 'ahad, ahad' in sermons and sirah study; the one who gives the call to prayer, the role he held, is called the mu'adhdhin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banu Hashim. Your line was: protected by love. Who did you thank for standing by you without agreeing? Day seven hundred thirty-six.

Abu Talib could shield his nephew. Not everyone who believed had an uncle like that. Some had no clan to stand behind them at all. Some were owned. Midday in the open valley of Mecca, the hottest hour. The ground burns. A man lies on his back on it, held there by a heavy stone on his chest, and the man who owns him stands over him, waiting for him to give in. Today: Bilal.
screen: `NOT EVERYONE HAD A SHIELD.` → `MIDDAY, BURNING GROUND.` → `A STONE ON HIS CHEST.`

segments.voice: Bilal ibn Rabah was enslaved in Mecca, the property of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and he had come to believe. Ibn Ishaq tells what Umayyah did. He would bring Bilal out in the heat of the day, throw him on his back in the open valley, and have a great rock laid on his chest. Then he would tell him: you will stay like this until you die, or until you deny Muhammad and worship the idols of Quraysh. And Bilal, under the stone, would say one word. Ahad. Ahad. One. One. He didn't argue. He didn't make a speech. He had almost no breath to make one with. He said one word, and it carried his whole answer to the idols: one God, not many. It is the same word that closes the first verse of a short surah of the Qur'an, which Pickthall translates: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" The sirah goes on: Abu Bakr passed by while this was happening, and he bought Bilal from Umayyah and set him free. Yesterday a clan head shielded the Prophet. Today a friend uses his wealth to shield a slave. Later in the story, al-Bukhari's reports name Bilal as the one who gave the call to prayer, the voice that called the believers in Medina. The man who could only manage one word under a stone became the voice that called them to prayer. That is for later. Today, there is only the heat, the stone, and the word.
screen: `BILAL, ENSLAVED TO UMAYYAH.` · `THE ROCK IN THE MIDDAY SUN.` · `AHAD, AHAD: ONE, ONE.` · `ABU BAKR SETS HIM FREE.` · then, large: `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE!`

segments.voice: The practice: say one word of faith. Settle and breathe. Choose one word that holds what you most trust: for Bilal it was ahad. If you're Muslim, you might choose ahad too. If not, choose your own one word: a name, a value, a promise. Breathe in, and on the out-breath say it, softly or silently. Let it be the whole prayer, or the whole thought. When the mind wanders, come back to the one word. The bell holds the time.
Bilal. The enslaved believer who, under a rock in the midday sun, said only ahad, one, until Abu Bakr bought his freedom. Today's word.
Your line: ahad. Today, when things press on you, come back to one word, and let it hold you steady. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: Sumayyah, the first martyr
737.hook: Sumayyah bint Khayyat, killed for her faith, is remembered as the first martyr of Islam
737.carry: the first to give her life
737.howItsDone: Muslims remember Sumayyah, the mother of Ammar ibn Yasir, in sirah lessons and sermons on the early persecution in Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilal under the rock in the sun. Your line was: ahad. One. Did you say your one word of faith, out loud or under your breath? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

A father, a mother, and their son. When Ibn Ishaq comes to the worst of the persecution in Mecca, he names this family together: Yasir, his wife, and their son Ammar. Men from the clan of Makhzum have taken them out into the heat of the city to make them give up the new faith. The mother has no powerful family to come and pull her away. Her name is Sumayyah bint Khayyat. The early biographers give her only a few lines, and tradition has kept those lines and retold them. Today: Sumayyah.
screen: `A FATHER, A MOTHER, A SON.` → `NO CLAN TO PULL HER AWAY.` → `SUMAYYAH BINT KHAYYAT.`

segments.voice: Start with who she was. The sirah books say she had been a servant in a household of Makhzum, married Yasir, a man from outside Mecca who lived there under that clan's protection, and had a son, Ammar. So when the family became Muslim, nobody stood between them and the clan. Bilal yesterday had no tribe behind him either. Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh turned hardest on the Muslims who had no clan to protect them. Ibn Majah reports from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that Sumayyah was among the first to make their Islam public, not just to hold it quietly. Then the end. Ibn Ishaq says the family was tortured in the heat of Mecca, and that Sumayyah was killed because she would accept nothing but Islam. Ibn Sa'd adds that Abu Jahl, one of the leaders of Quraysh, struck her with a spear, and he calls her the first martyr in Islam. That's where the title comes from. The Arabic word for martyr is shahid, and the same word is used in the Qur'an for a witness. A martyr, in that sense, is someone whose life becomes testimony. Notice how little the sources hand us. No speech. No last words. Just a choice, held under pressure, by someone the powerful thought did not matter. Tradition remembers her for it: in Ibn Sa'd's telling, the first life given in Islam was a woman's, and she was not one of the powerful.
screen: `A SERVANT, A WIFE, A MOTHER.` · `NO CLAN TO SHIELD HER.` · `SHE WOULD ACCEPT NOTHING BUT ISLAM.` · `SHAHID: A MARTYR, A WITNESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember someone who suffered for what they believed. Sit, and let your breathing settle. It can be someone from history, from any faith or none, or someone in your own family: a grandparent who kept their faith quietly in a hard place, a person who lost a job for refusing to lie. Hold their face, or their name, if you don't know the face. Say the name once, softly. You don't need to know how the story ended. Just keep them company for a minute, the way people have kept Sumayyah's name. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Sumayyah. Sumayyah bint Khayyat, mother of Ammar, killed in Mecca for her faith, whom Ibn Sa'd calls the first martyr in Islam. Today's word.
Your line: the first to give her life. Today, notice one person around you whom others overlook, and treat what they say as if it matters. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

738.title: Yasir's family
738.hook: the Prophet ﷺ passes the tortured family and says: patience, family of Yasir, your meeting is the garden (sirah)
738.howItsDone: Muslims retell the Prophet's words to the family of Yasir in sermons on patience under hardship, and Ammar's story is a standard text in discussions of what a person forced to speak against their faith is excused.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sumayyah. Your line was: the first to give her life. Whose name did you keep company with, and did you notice someone others overlook? Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

What can be said to people you cannot rescue? Ibn Ishaq keeps one answer. The family of Yasir is being tortured in Mecca, and someone walks past who knows them: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He has no army. He has no clan strong enough to march into Makhzum's affairs and take the family home. He can't untie them. So he stops, and speaks, in a sentence short enough to carry: patience, family of Yasir, your meeting place is the garden. Today: Yasir's family, and what you can say when you can't fix anything.
screen: `PEOPLE YOU CANNOT RESCUE.` → `HE CAN'T UNTIE THEM.` → `PATIENCE, FAMILY OF YASIR.`

segments.voice: Look at the sentence itself. It names them. Not the believers in general, not the oppressed of Mecca: the family of Yasir. Whoever is suffering hears their own name. Then a word, sabr, patience, which in Arabic means holding steady, not waiting politely. Then a promise: the garden, the word the Qur'an uses for paradise, as the place where they will meet. He doesn't tell them it will stop soon. It doesn't. Ibn Sa'd says Yasir also died under the torture. Then the son. Ammar was pushed so far that he said what his torturers demanded, words against the Prophet and praise for the idols. Al-Hakim reports that he came to the Prophet weeping. And the Prophet asked him one question: how do you find your heart? Ammar said: at peace with faith. And he was told: if they come back, say it again. Commentators such as al-Tabari connect this with surah sixteen, verse one hundred six, which excuses the one who is forced to speak disbelief while the heart stays at rest in faith. So in one family the sirah holds two kinds of faithfulness. The parents held their ground to the end. The son broke in words and kept his heart, and was not condemned for it. Both were met with mercy, not a ranking. That's the shape of the sentence on the hot ground: name the people, ask them to hold steady, and point beyond the day.
screen: `IT NAMES THEM.` · `SABR: HOLDING STEADY.` · `HOW DO YOU FIND YOUR HEART?` · `TWO KINDS OF FAITHFULNESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: console a suffering family. Settle first. Bring to mind a family you know who is carrying something heavy: an illness, a loss, a son in trouble. You may not be able to fix any of it. Neither could he. Use the minute to find what you can say. Their names, first. Then a few true words, nothing you'd have to take back. If you can, send it today: a short message, a call, a knock on the door. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Yasir's family. Yasir, Sumayyah and their son Ammar, tortured in Mecca, to whom the Prophet said: patience, your meeting place is the garden. Today's word.
Your line: patience, family of yasir. Today, when someone tells you what they're going through, say their name back to them before you say anything else. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

739.title: Ibn Mas'ud aloud
739.hook: the small shepherd Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recites Surah ar-Rahman aloud at the Ka'ba and is beaten (sirah)
739.howItsDone: Muslims recite the Qur'an aloud in prayer and in gatherings, and Ibn Mas'ud is remembered among the companions known for their recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasir's family on the hot ground. Your line was: patience, family of yasir. Did you say someone's name back to them before anything else? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

A small circle of the Prophet's companions in Mecca, talking low. Ibn Ishaq gives their worry in a sentence: Quraysh have never heard this Qur'an recited openly to them. Who will make them hear it? One voice answers: I will. It belongs to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a shepherd, slight and thin-legged, with no strong clan behind him. The others object. They want someone whose family will step in if the crowd turns on him. He goes anyway. Today: Ibn Mas'ud.
screen: `WHO WILL MAKE THEM HEAR IT?` → `"I WILL."` → `A SHEPHERD WITH NO CLAN.`

segments.voice: The next morning, Ibn Ishaq says, he goes to the Ka'ba while the leaders of Quraysh are sitting in their meeting places, stands at the Maqam, and raises his voice. What he chooses to recite is the opening of surah fifty-five, ar-Rahman. In Pickthall's words: "The Beneficent Hath made known the Qur'an." Notice the choice. Not a warning. Not a threat. A surah that opens with the name of mercy and goes on listing gifts: the sun and moon, the sky raised up, the fruit and the palm, with a refrain that comes back again and again: "Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?" The crowd works out what he is reading and gets up and strikes him in the face. He keeps reciting as far as he can before he goes back to his friends, his face marked. They say: this is what we were afraid of. And Ibn Ishaq gives his answer: God's enemies were never smaller in his eyes than now, and if they like, he'll do it again tomorrow. There's one more detail, from Musnad Ahmad. Once, some companions laughed at how thin Ibn Mas'ud's legs were, and the Prophet said those legs would weigh heavier on the scale than the mountain of Uhud. Put the two together. The man some laughed at was the one who carried the words of mercy out loud, and paid for it, and offered to go back.
screen: `AT THE MAQAM, IN THE MORNING.` · `HE CHOSE AR-RAHMAN.` · `STRUCK IN THE FACE, STILL RECITING.` · `THIN LEGS, HEAVY ON THE SCALE.`

segments.voice: The practice: recite something aloud, without fear. Choose a few lines that matter to you: a verse, a prayer you already know, a poem you love, a line your grandmother used to say. Find a place where you can be heard, even if only by the walls. Then say it in your full voice, not a whisper. Slowly, so each word lands. If your voice shakes, let it shake. Say it twice. Then sit quietly and notice how the room sounds after. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Mas'ud. A shepherd with no strong clan, who recited surah ar-Rahman openly at the Ka'ba, was beaten, and offered to do it again. Today's word.
Your line: he recited it aloud. Today, read one line you love out loud where someone else might hear it, and don't lower your voice when they do. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

740.title: Hamzah's anger
740.hook: his uncle Hamzah hears of an insult to his nephew and declares his Islam (sirah)
740.howItsDone: Muslims honor Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib as the Prophet's uncle and a defender of the early community, calling him the lion of God, and his story is told in sirah classes and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Mas'ud at the Ka'ba. Your line was: he recited it aloud. What did you say out loud, and did you soften it? Day seven hundred forty.

A hunter comes home with his bow over his shoulder. He's been out in the desert all day. His habit, Ibn Ishaq says, is to walk around the Ka'ba before he goes home and greet the men sitting there. But today a woman stops him on the way. She is a freedwoman who lives near Safa, and she has just watched something she can't keep to herself. That morning, Abu Jahl came across the Prophet, peace be upon him, there by the hill, insulted him to his face and abused him, and the Prophet said nothing back. The hunter is Hamzah, the Prophet's uncle. Today: Hamzah's anger.
screen: `A HUNTER COMES HOME.` → `A WOMAN STOPS HIM.` → `HIS NEPHEW WAS INSULTED.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says Hamzah was filled with fury. He didn't go around the Ka'ba greeting anyone. He walked straight to where Abu Jahl sat among the men of Quraysh, stood over him, and struck him with his bow, hard enough to wound his head. Then he said: will you insult him, when I follow his religion and say what he says? Strike me back, if you can. Men from Abu Jahl's clan stood up to defend him. Abu Jahl stopped them. Leave Abu Umarah alone, he said, for by God, I insulted his nephew badly. Then the sirah notes the shift in the town. Quraysh understood that the Prophet now had a strong defender, and some of their harassment eased. Hamzah is remembered by Muslims as the lion of God, asad Allah. That's where today's line comes from. But notice how he came in: not after a long study, but in a burst of loyalty and rage. Some versions of the story go on to say that, afterward, he was troubled about what he had said in the heat of the moment, and asked God for guidance, until his heart settled. If that's so, the anger opened the door, and something quieter had to walk him through it. The insult was meant to shrink a man who wouldn't answer back. It brought his uncle into the faith.
screen: `STRAIGHT TO ABU JAHL.` · `I FOLLOW HIS RELIGION. STRIKE ME BACK.` · `LEAVE HIM: I INSULTED HIS NEPHEW.` · `ANGER OPENED THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The practice: defend someone insulted. You don't need a bow. Sit, and breathe, and think back over the last few weeks. Was someone mocked in front of you, at work, in a group chat, at the dinner table, and nobody said anything? Maybe you didn't either. Find the moment. Then find one sentence, calm and clear, that you could have said, or still can. Not an insult back. Just a line that stands next to them. Say it quietly to yourself until it feels like yours. The bell holds the time.
Hamzah's anger. The Prophet's uncle hears his nephew was insulted, strikes Abu Jahl with his bow, and declares that he follows his religion. Today's word.
Your line: the lion comes in. Today, if you hear someone put down behind their back, say one calm sentence that stands with them. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: Umar comes in
741.hook: the fierce Umar, angry, reads Ta-Ha at his sister's house and goes to declare his faith (sirah)
741.tomorrow: To the land of a just king
741.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Umar's conversion in sirah lessons and sermons, and some teachers point to it as an example of a page of the Qur'an changing a heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hamzah's anger. Your line was: the lion comes in. Did you hear someone put down, and did you find your one calm sentence? Day seven hundred forty-one.

A man walks through Mecca with a sword at his side and a plan to end the whole thing. Ibn Ishaq says Umar ibn al-Khattab set out that day intending to kill the Prophet, peace be upon him. On the way a man named Nu'aym stops him and asks where he's going. When Umar tells him, Nu'aym says: you'd do better to look at your own family. Your sister Fatimah and her husband have already followed him. Umar turns around. Today: Ta-Ha.
screen: `A SWORD AND A PLAN.` → `NU'AYM STOPS HIM.` → `LOOK AT YOUR OWN FAMILY.`

segments.voice: At his sister's door he hears a murmur. Inside, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt is reading to Fatimah and her husband Sa'id from a written page: the opening of surah Ta-Ha. When Umar knocks, Khabbab hides, and Fatimah slips the page out of sight. Umar storms in, demanding to know what that sound was. He grabs his brother-in-law, and when his sister steps between them, he strikes her and draws blood. Then she says it plainly: yes, we are Muslims. Do what you like. And something in him stops. Ibn Ishaq says that when he saw the blood, he was sorry, and he asked for the page. Fatimah wouldn't hand it over until he had washed. He washed. Then he read. The opening of Ta-Ha says, in paraphrase, that the Qur'an was not sent down to make the Prophet miserable, but as a reminder for the one who fears God, from the one who created the earth and the high heavens. Umar read it and said, Ibn Ishaq reports: how fine and noble this speech is. Khabbab came out of hiding. And Umar asked where the Prophet was, went to the house near Safa where the believers met, and declared his faith there. Notice the order. Nu'aym turned him around, but the sword and the anger came with him, until his sister stood her ground and he saw her blood. Then he had to wash before he could read. And then a page did what an argument hadn't.
screen: `A MURMUR BEHIND THE DOOR.` · `HIS SISTER STANDS HER GROUND.` · `WASH, THEN READ.` · `HOW FINE AND NOBLE THIS SPEECH IS.`

segments.voice: The practice: let a page change your mind. Take a page that you've already made up your mind about: a passage from a holy book, a letter from someone you're angry with, an article from the side you don't agree with. Before you read, do something to clear the decks: wash your hands, or just put your phone face down. Then read slowly, one line at a time, as if you'd never seen it. Look for one sentence that's finer than you expected. Just one. Hold it while you sit. The bell holds the time.
Ta-Ha. Umar ibn al-Khattab, on his way to kill the Prophet, reads this surah's opening at his sister's house and goes to declare his faith. Today's word.
Your line: the page turned him. Today, read one page you'd normally skip, slowly, and find the line in it that's better than you thought. Day seven hundred forty-one.

screen: `DAY 741 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TO THE LAND OF A JUST KING.`

742.title: To the land of a just king
742.hook: the Prophet ﷺ sends some to Abyssinia, where a king rules who wrongs no one (sirah)
742.howItsDone: Muslims know this as the emigration to Abyssinia (al-Habashah), told in sirah lessons as the community's first hijrah, and the Negus is remembered with honor for sheltering them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ta-Ha. Your line was: the page turned him. Which page did you read slowly, and what line in it surprised you? Day seven hundred forty-two.

A leader who can't protect his people has a hard choice. He can tell them to hold on. He can tell them to fight. Or he can tell them to leave. Ibn Ishaq says that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, saw what his companions were suffering, and saw that he could not shield them, he pointed them across the sea, to Abyssinia. His reason wasn't that the land was Muslim. It wasn't. His reason was the man who ruled it. Today: hijrah.
screen: `HOLD ON, FIGHT, OR LEAVE?` → `ACROSS THE SEA.` → `BECAUSE OF THE KING.`

segments.voice: Here is what Ibn Ishaq has him say, in paraphrase: if you go to Abyssinia, you'll find a king there under whom no one is wronged. It is a land of truthfulness, until God makes a way out for you from what you're in. Look at what he praises. Not the king's religion; he is a Christian, ruling a Christian land. Not his wealth or his army. Justice: in his land, no one is wronged. The Prophet trusted his people to a ruler of another faith because that ruler was fair. So some of the Muslims went. Ibn Ishaq calls it the first emigration in Islam, the first hijrah, before the later one to Medina. Among those who went, he names Uthman ibn Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's own daughter. This wasn't sending strangers away. He sent his child. And Umm Salamah, who went too, later remembered what they found. In the report kept in Musnad Ahmad, she says they came to the best of neighbors, that they were safe in their faith, and worshipped God without being harmed or hearing anything they hated. Safe in their faith, in someone else's country. The story doesn't end quietly; tomorrow, Quraysh come after them. But for now, notice the picture: the first hijrah was Muslims running for safety to the court of a just king.
screen: `NO ONE IS WRONGED THERE.` · `HE PRAISES JUSTICE, NOT RELIGION.` · `HE SENT HIS OWN DAUGHTER.` · `SAFE IN THEIR FAITH, FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a just person. Settle into your breath. This time, look for fairness from someone who owed you nothing: a person outside your circle, of another faith or background, who held the rules level when it would have been easy to tilt them. An official who processed your papers honestly. A referee who called it straight against the home crowd. A landlord who gave back the whole deposit. Notice exactly what they did, and what it might have cost them. Then thank them, if you can reach them, naming the fair thing. If you can't, say their name and the thanks quietly now. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Hijrah. The Prophet sends companions to Abyssinia, the first emigration in Islam, to a king who, he says, rules so that no one is wronged. Today's word.
Your line: a just king. Today, when you have a little power over someone, a decision, a grade, a turn, use it so that no one is wronged. Day seven hundred forty-two.
